Cautiously dovish tone with a rules-consistent tilt. The 25 bp cut to a 4.5–4.75% funds-rate range, coupled with “risks roughly in balance,” fits Taylor-rule style reaction functions when inflation is moving toward target and the unemployment rate has edged up (Clarida, Galí, and Gertler). The emphasis on inflation’s progress yet “somewhat elevated” level echoes inflation-forecast–targeting frameworks that put weight on projected inflation relative to the 2% goal (Svensson and Woodford, 2005). Operationally, lowering the interest on reserve balances to 4.65% and using standing repo and reverse-repo facilities reflects the modern channel system and administered-rate implementation discussed by Goodfriend (2002). Maintaining balance-sheet runoff while easing the policy rate is consistent with the multi‑instrument view in which the short rate manages aggregate demand while the balance sheet influences term premia and market functioning (Cúrdia and Woodford, and the broader QE literature). Finally, cost‑channel models suggest modest rate reductions can lower working‑capital costs and marginal cost pressures, complementing disinflation progress (Christiano, Eichenbaum, and Evans, 2005; Ravenna and Walsh, 2006). Net effect: a mildly positive shift in stance for growth with a still vigilant posture on inflation.
